cells.tense: You are the one who keeps the roof up, and it does not cost you your softness.
cells.ask: Let one person carry the next thing you would have taken; stay while they finish it.
cells.core:
When pressure comes, you can hold the shape of it without going stiff and without falling apart. You stay in touch with the people around you while you bear it, which is rarer than bearing it alone. It runs the way it should: the weight arrives, you take it, and you are still yourself on the other side.

The place it slips is naming. You take the weight, then go quiet and let it look like nothing happened. Try handing one small thing back to the person it belongs to. Stay in the room while they handle it, and do not take it back. That is what keeps this steady: the credit stays with you, and the load gets shared instead of absorbed.
cells.sheetLine: You hold the weight and stay soft. Let someone else carry one piece.
cells.verb: seeing the whole thing through and knowing there is nothing left to add
cells.place: the room where you take the weight and hold it steady

cells.tense: You are bracing for weight that has not come, and the bracing has become its own work.
cells.ask: Name one thing already handled, then set one worry down for an hour and do the next plain task.
cells.core:
A body like this meets trouble when it shows up, bears what's real, and comes out the far side intact. Lately the trouble hasn't shown up. Contingencies, rehearsals, the shape of the next hard thing — you take them on before they exist, so the waiting itself becomes the job. Some of that readiness is exactly right, and some is aimed at a future that cannot be written in yet.

What it costs is the present, which sits unheld while you prepare for later. Nothing about your strength disappears when you stop bracing. Pick one worry, write it down, leave it alone for an hour. Do the next ordinary thing in front of you with both hands. That is the same strength doing less work, not a different person.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding what hasn't come. Set one worry down for an hour.

cells.tense: You stopped letting the weight show, and you would call that just getting on with it.
cells.ask: Tell one person one true sentence about what is heavy, no fixing asked for, and stay in the room.
cells.core:
You can still carry a great deal, and you do. What has gone quiet is letting anyone see it happen. You hold the load on your own, say nothing about it, and the day moves on, and nobody in the room knows what is being borne. Carrying well does not mean carrying less — it means carrying it in contact with somebody.

Being seen while carrying is not the same as needing rescue. Pick one person, one true sentence about what is heavy, nothing asked of them. Then stop and let them hear it without rushing to make it lighter. That contact is what keeps your strength from becoming a wall you hold up by yourself. Being known while you hold is the point, not holding less.
cells.sheetLine: You carry it unseen. Say one true sentence to one person.

cells.tense: You already steady the room when you walk in, and you would say you are just being practical.
cells.ask: Say out loud one ordinary thing you do that steadies someone, and put your name on it today.
cells.core:
People settle when you are in the room, and you would describe that as nothing — just being sensible. The learning is already done in you: what breaks under weight, what holds, how much you can take. It runs through how you wait, how you do not flinch, how you keep the room from tipping. None of it is credited to you as something you do.

Naming it is not showing off. It is putting your own name back on work you have been calling logistics. Today, catch one plain thing — the way you hold a silence, the way you stay — and say, in a sentence you would actually use, that you do it. The light is already on; this just says whose it is.
